### Beyond Proficient

::: {.meta}
Science MCA-IV, spring 2025. Grades 5, 8, and high school.
:::

Minnesota reports school science performance as a percent proficient. That number turns out to be a near-deterministic function of two things the state also publishes: a school's average scale score and its standard deviation. A model using only those two inputs predicts the reported proficiency rate at r = 0.965.

Which means proficiency rates exaggerate real differences. Two schools nine scale points apart report 17% and 43%.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects.qmd){.view}

### Minnesota Early Learning Scholarships

::: {.meta}
County-level awards across five fiscal years.
:::

Minnesota publishes scholarship awards by county but not the rate at which awarded scholarships go unused. Deriving that rate, and a per-county baseline index, made visible which counties are most exposed to the funding contraction that follows a large one-time appropriation.

[See the analysis and dashboard](projects.qmd#minnesota-early-learning-scholarships){.view}
:::
:::

## How I work

I state the method where the reader can see it. Suppressed cells get counted rather than quietly dropped. Derived measures get labeled as derived. When two test series are not comparable, I do not draw a trend line across them.

That last one matters more than it sounds. Science MCA-IV replaced MCA-III in 2025 against a different set of standards, so there is no valid multi-year science trend in Minnesota right now. A dashboard that showed one would look better and be wrong.

I write assessment items, which means I read score reports differently than most analysts do. I know what a reporting category is built to support and what it is not, and I would rather say plainly where the public data stops than point at something adjacent.
